compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional tagline review, either person might ask what the team wants the message to say or how an audience might read it. Both questions are relevant, and either person can ask both.

The shared N and F help explain where the descriptions overlap. The two differences still need separate questions: does attention turn more readily to external interaction or internal reflection, and does the person prefer to leave the outward decision open or give it shape?

### ENFP and INFJ: in one discussion, how options get explored and wording judged

In this fictional tagline review, both people have the same brief, three options, audience, deadline and decision authority. One approach keeps workable alternatives open for further feedback. Another records a provisional choice and states what evidence would reopen it. Either person can use either approach.

Keeping the discussion open can delay a decision. Committing early can rule out a promising option before enough is known. The trade-off depends on the information available and how reversible the choice is.

Either person could add an option or narrow the list to one. The number of candidates reflects the brief, deadline and decision process. It cannot identify a type.

### ENFP and INFJ: why the categories correspond and the attitudes reverse

In the notation used here, both stacks list Intuition, Feeling, Thinking and Sensing in that order. The attitudes differ at each position: Ne and Ni, Fi and Fe, Te and Ti, and Si and Se. Ne and Ni refer to different forms of Intuition within the model.

In type dynamics, E/I determines the attitude of the dominant process, and J/P tells you whether the process shown to the outside world is a perceiving or judging process. ENFP’s outward process is dominant Ne, while INFJ’s is auxiliary Fe. This explains the stacks without implying an order of actions.

In the model, Ne explores connections and possibilities, while Ni brings clues together into an internal interpretation. Fi weighs a choice against personally held values, while Fe attends to shared values and interpersonal consequences. All four labels describe processes in the model. They do not establish what either person will do in a meeting.

The model gives the two types different outward processes. For ENFP that is Ne, a perceiving process. For INFJ it is Fe, a judging process. This distinction tells you more about the notation than about who will speak up or finish first.

The fourth position does not measure ability. INFJ’s Se does not tell you what someone will notice in a room, and ENFP’s Si does not tell you which details they will remember.

Whether the third is marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform: for ENFP's Te and INFJ's Ti, some tables give only the process name without an attitude. When a version differs, check whether it names its source, then read the pair through the first two positions. This page takes the common version and does not present the marking as the Foundation's only reading. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial fiction, used only to practise telling apart which kind of evidence each may take first, corresponding to no real project or person. Either type may make the other's choice in any segment; the division should follow who knows, who is present and who normally handles external contact, not type.

Working together on brand content, one may prefer to spread the possibility out and the other to pull the wording onto one line. This is not a fixed division, but it is worth stating in advance: who closes at which stage, and whether anything can be reopened after the close.

### ENFP and INFJ: three versions of a brand line

In this fictional review, both people consider the same three taglines for distributors. One option describes ingredients, one describes when the product is used and one expresses a brand value. Either person can suggest a fourth, check for likely misreadings or narrow the list.

Leaving options open gives new evidence room to matter. Setting a provisional choice can make the next step clearer. Which approach helps depends on whether the team already has enough information.

A workable checkpoint: before finalising, ask several people close to the target audience to repeat each candidate under conditions as similar as possible — the same explanation of order, the same time limit, the same follow-up questions; rotate the order between people so that only the first one is not the only one remembered. If the same misreading recurs across different people, that is a signal the sentence needs rewriting; one person's single deviation is not enough to eliminate a candidate, and may reflect their own experience or attention. The remaining candidates are then ranked by value consistency and audience understanding, with room for both kinds of judgement.

### ENFP and INFJ: whether to write "number one" into the line

(Fictional scene) A partner insists on "number one seller". The same factual threshold comes first, for both types: verify the statistical scope, period and definition behind the claim, and whether they support the words "number one". Without checkable data, "many people buy it again" is not more reliable because the wording is softer — it is equally a factual claim and equally needs evidence.

In the fictional discussion, either person might ask whether they can stand behind a wording and whether it honours the expectations the team has set with its audience. Once the facts support the claim, these questions can guide the choice between defensible alternatives.

The disagreement looks like a question of who is listening, but the premise is still factual verification. A workable approach has each write one sentence on how we answer if challenged, and both sentences must be supported by existing evidence; whichever cannot be written goes back to evidence first rather than being deleted. Once the evidence is in place, choose the wording by value consistency and how the audience is likely to understand it. That avoids treating the softer phrasing as a free pass, and avoids treating a choice of expression as a factual judgement.

### ENFP and INFJ: two old friends fall out, and you are in the middle

In this fictional example, two longtime friends fall out after a collaboration and both contact you. One way to help is to ask what each person understood and look for other explanations. Another is to reflect on whether the dispute started with this event or grew over time. Either person can do both. The order does not identify ENFP or INFJ.

Passing accounts between the friends can deepen misunderstandings. Assuming the conflict has deep roots can overlook a simple mix-up. Check what each person actually said before drawing conclusions.

A check can run like this: separate first what is confirmed fact from what is feeling and inference. If the factual part needs relaying, get the person's consent and ask them to confirm the retelling is accurate; the steadier approach is to let the person communicate themselves and only carry the message. Feelings and inferences are better said by the person themselves — relaying distorts them and easily makes both sides feel you have picked one.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is word count. An ENFP may talk more among strangers, an INFJ may talk longer in a small group, but neither is evidence for E or I. An ENFP may have nothing to say after a long meeting, and an INFJ may grab the floor at a topic meeting; word count depends more on setting, familiarity and the day's state.

The second gives depth of thought to I. Both care about what a sentence means underneath; the difference is whether that caring goes into expanding directions or closing onto one line. Depth is not exclusive to introversion, and questioning is not a patent of extraversion.

The third treats repeated revision as unprofessional. An ENFP revising again may be looking for the line they genuinely endorse; an INFJ revising again may have noticed one more listener left out. That is a way of working and the basis of judgement at the time, not a grade of ability, and it cannot be read backwards into job suitability — the number of revisions also depends on the review process, the decision chain and the quality of feedback.

The fourth uses the number of candidates or the order of actions as a test. More or fewer before and after a meeting depends on the width of the brief, who is present and who holds sign-off; who speaks first and who finalises first depends on role and experience. Both observations describe a meeting, not a person's type.

body: In a fictional tagline review, either person might ask what the team wants the message to say or how an audience might read it. Both questions are relevant, and either person can ask both.

The shared N and F help explain where the descriptions overlap. The two differences still need separate questions: does attention turn more readily to external interaction or internal reflection, and does the person prefer to leave the outward decision open or give it shape?
### ENFP and INFJ: in one discussion, how options get explored and wording judged

In this fictional tagline review, both people have the same brief, three options, audience, deadline and decision authority. One approach keeps workable alternatives open for further feedback. Another records a provisional choice and states what evidence would reopen it. Either person can use either approach.

Keeping the discussion open can delay a decision. Committing early can rule out a promising option before enough is known. The trade-off depends on the information available and how reversible the choice is.
Either person could add an option or narrow the list to one. The number of candidates reflects the brief, deadline and decision process. It cannot identify a type.
### ENFP and INFJ: why the categories correspond and the attitudes reverse

In the notation used here, both stacks list Intuition, Feeling, Thinking and Sensing in that order. The attitudes differ at each position: Ne and Ni, Fi and Fe, Te and Ti, and Si and Se. Ne and Ni refer to different forms of Intuition within the model.

body: Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial fiction, used only to practise telling apart which kind of evidence each may take first, corresponding to no real project or person. Either type may make the other's choice in any segment; the division should follow who knows, who is present and who normally handles external contact, not type.

Working together on brand content, one may prefer to spread the possibility out and the other to pull the wording onto one line. This is not a fixed division, but it is worth stating in advance: who closes at which stage, and whether anything can be reopened after the close.
### ENFP and INFJ: three versions of a brand line

In this fictional review, both people consider the same three taglines for distributors. One option describes ingredients, one describes when the product is used and one expresses a brand value. Either person can suggest a fourth, check for likely misreadings or narrow the list.
Leaving options open gives new evidence room to matter. Setting a provisional choice can make the next step clearer. Which approach helps depends on whether the team already has enough information.

A workable checkpoint: before finalising, ask several people close to the target audience to repeat each candidate under conditions as similar as possible — the same explanation of order, the same time limit, the same follow-up questions; rotate the order between people so that only the first one is not the only one remembered. If the same misreading recurs across different people, that is a signal the sentence needs rewriting; one person's single deviation is not enough to eliminate a candidate, and may reflect their own experience or attention. The remaining candidates are then ranked by value consistency and audience understanding, with room for both kinds of judgement.
### ENFP and INFJ: whether to write "number one" into the line

(Fictional scene) A partner insists on "number one seller". The same factual threshold comes first, for both types: verify the statistical scope, period and definition behind the claim, and whether they support the words "number one". Without checkable data, "many people buy it again" is not more reliable because the wording is softer — it is equally a factual claim and equally needs evidence.

In the fictional discussion, either person might ask whether they can stand behind a wording and whether it honours the expectations the team has set with its audience. Once the facts support the claim, these questions can guide the choice between defensible alternatives.

The disagreement looks like a question of who is listening, but the premise is still factual verification. A workable approach has each write one sentence on how we answer if challenged, and both sentences must be supported by existing evidence; whichever cannot be written goes back to evidence first rather than being deleted. Once the evidence is in place, choose the wording by value consistency and how the audience is likely to understand it. That avoids treating the softer phrasing as a free pass, and avoids treating a choice of expression as a factual judgement.
### ENFP and INFJ: two old friends fall out, and you are in the middle

In this fictional example, two longtime friends fall out after a collaboration and both contact you. One way to help is to ask what each person understood and look for other explanations. Another is to reflect on whether the dispute started with this event or grew over time. Either person can do both. The order does not identify ENFP or INFJ.
Passing accounts between the friends can deepen misunderstandings. Assuming the conflict has deep roots can overlook a simple mix-up. Check what each person actually said before drawing conclusions.

A check can run like this: separate first what is confirmed fact from what is feeling and inference. If the factual part needs relaying, get the person's consent and ask them to confirm the retelling is accurate; the steadier approach is to let the person communicate themselves and only carry the message. Feelings and inferences are better said by the person themselves — relaying distorts them and easily makes both sides feel you have picked one.

body: The first misread is word count. An ENFP may talk more among strangers, an INFJ may talk longer in a small group, but neither is evidence for E or I. An ENFP may have nothing to say after a long meeting, and an INFJ may grab the floor at a topic meeting; word count depends more on setting, familiarity and the day's state.

The second gives depth of thought to I. Both care about what a sentence means underneath; the difference is whether that caring goes into expanding directions or closing onto one line. Depth is not exclusive to introversion, and questioning is not a patent of extraversion.

The third treats repeated revision as unprofessional. An ENFP revising again may be looking for the line they genuinely endorse; an INFJ revising again may have noticed one more listener left out. That is a way of working and the basis of judgement at the time, not a grade of ability, and it cannot be read backwards into job suitability — the number of revisions also depends on the review process, the decision chain and the quality of feedback.

The fourth uses the number of candidates or the order of actions as a test. More or fewer before and after a meeting depends on the width of the brief, who is present and who holds sign-off; who speaks first and who finalises first depends on role and experience. Both observations describe a meeting, not a person's type.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank and the circumstances: the same version, the same language, the same scoring definition; and whether you were thinking of your own habit or of the way the job requires you to present. People who work in content are often asked to give a few more directions, and such demands may affect how you understand the items and recall your own behaviour, though it cannot be assumed which side they push you toward.

The practice does not need counts, only reasons. Take a few real finalisation meetings and write four lines for each: which stage it was at (gathering material, writing candidates, rehearsing reactions, finalising, answering challenges); what role you held; what the constraints were (who the audience was, who held sign-off, how long until the deadline); and why the trade-off went that way. Look for the recurring reason — whether this is the line we endorse, or how this line will be read by whom. The two axes can also be recorded separately: on E/I, whether you have more energy after talking with people or need to be alone; on J/P, whether you would rather settle a deliverable version or keep room to change. Read both across several situations rather than from a single reaction. These notes serve reflection, are not scored and do not assign a type.

Record counterexamples too: using the other kind of evidence on the same matter shows both approaches are within reach. An ENFP will also close before a deadline, and an INFJ will also keep diverging when information is sufficient. If the item bank gives dimension scores, near a boundary only means the result sits close to a threshold under this item bank; it does not prove you switch freely between two modes, and it does not mean two types both hold.

Working together on brand content, one may prefer to spread the possibility out and the other to pull the wording onto one line. This is not a fixed division, but it is worth stating in advance: who closes at which stage, and whether anything can be reopened after the close.

### ENFP and INFJ: three versions of a brand line

In this fictional review, both people consider the same three taglines for distributors. One option describes ingredients, one describes when the product is used and one expresses a brand value. Either person can suggest a fourth, check for likely misreadings or narrow the list.

Leaving options open gives new evidence room to matter. Setting a provisional choice can make the next step clearer. Which approach helps depends on whether the team already has enough information.

A workable checkpoint: before finalising, ask several people close to the target audience to repeat each candidate under conditions as similar as possible — the same explanation of order, the same time limit, the same follow-up questions; rotate the order between people so that only the first one is not the only one remembered. If the same misreading recurs across different people, that is a signal the sentence needs rewriting; one person's single deviation is not enough to eliminate a candidate, and may reflect their own experience or attention. The remaining candidates are then ranked by value consistency and audience understanding, with room for both kinds of judgement.

### ENFP and INFJ: whether to write "number one" into the line

(Fictional scene) A partner insists on "number one seller". The same factual threshold comes first, for both types: verify the statistical scope, period and definition behind the claim, and whether they support the words "number one". Without checkable data, "many people buy it again" is not more reliable because the wording is softer — it is equally a factual claim and equally needs evidence.

In the fictional discussion, either person might ask whether they can stand behind a wording and whether it honours the expectations the team has set with its audience. Once the facts support the claim, these questions can guide the choice between defensible alternatives.

The disagreement looks like a question of who is listening, but the premise is still factual verification. A workable approach has each write one sentence on how we answer if challenged, and both sentences must be supported by existing evidence; whichever cannot be written goes back to evidence first rather than being deleted. Once the evidence is in place, choose the wording by value consistency and how the audience is likely to understand it. That avoids treating the softer phrasing as a free pass, and avoids treating a choice of expression as a factual judgement.

### ENFP and INFJ: two old friends fall out, and you are in the middle

In this fictional example, two longtime friends fall out after a collaboration and both contact you. One way to help is to ask what each person understood and look for other explanations. Another is to reflect on whether the dispute started with this event or grew over time. Either person can do both. The order does not identify ENFP or INFJ.

Passing accounts between the friends can deepen misunderstandings. Assuming the conflict has deep roots can overlook a simple mix-up. Check what each person actually said before drawing conclusions.

A check can run like this: separate first what is confirmed fact from what is feeling and inference. If the factual part needs relaying, get the person's consent and ask them to confirm the retelling is accurate; the steadier approach is to let the person communicate themselves and only carry the message. Feelings and inferences are better said by the person themselves — relaying distorts them and easily makes both sides feel you have picked one.
sections.title: ENFP and INFJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The first misread is word count. An ENFP may talk more among strangers, an INFJ may talk longer in a small group, but neither is evidence for E or I. An ENFP may have nothing to say after a long meeting, and an INFJ may grab the floor at a topic meeting; word count depends more on setting, familiarity and the day's state.

The second gives depth of thought to I. Both care about what a sentence means underneath; the difference is whether that caring goes into expanding directions or closing onto one line. Depth is not exclusive to introversion, and questioning is not a patent of extraversion.

The third treats repeated revision as unprofessional. An ENFP revising again may be looking for the line they genuinely endorse; an INFJ revising again may have noticed one more listener left out. That is a way of working and the basis of judgement at the time, not a grade of ability, and it cannot be read backwards into job suitability — the number of revisions also depends on the review process, the decision chain and the quality of feedback.

The fourth uses the number of candidates or the order of actions as a test. More or fewer before and after a meeting depends on the width of the brief, who is present and who holds sign-off; who speaks first and who finalises first depends on role and experience. Both observations describe a meeting, not a person's type.
sections.title: ENFP and INFJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank and the circumstances: the same version, the same language, the same scoring definition; and whether you were thinking of your own habit or of the way the job requires you to present. People who work in content are often asked to give a few more directions, and such demands may affect how you understand the items and recall your own behaviour, though it cannot be assumed which side they push you toward.

The practice does not need counts, only reasons. Take a few real finalisation meetings and write four lines for each: which stage it was at (gathering material, writing candidates, rehearsing reactions, finalising, answering challenges); what role you held; what the constraints were (who the audience was, who held sign-off, how long until the deadline); and why the trade-off went that way. Look for the recurring reason — whether this is the line we endorse, or how this line will be read by whom. The two axes can also be recorded separately: on E/I, whether you have more energy after talking with people or need to be alone; on J/P, whether you would rather settle a deliverable version or keep room to change. Read both across several situations rather than from a single reaction. These notes serve reflection, are not scored and do not assign a type.

Record counterexamples too: using the other kind of evidence on the same matter shows both approaches are within reach. An ENFP will also close before a deadline, and an INFJ will also keep diverging when information is sufficient. If the item bank gives dimension scores, near a boundary only means the result sits close to a threshold under this item bank; it does not prove you switch freely between two modes, and it does not mean two types both hold.

items.answer:
ENFP and INFJ share N and F and differ on Extraversion/Introversion and Judging/Perceiving.

E/I describes whether attention and energy generally turn outward or inward. J/P describes how the person prefers to engage with the outside world, with an outward decision or with options left open. Either type can broaden or narrow a shortlist.
items.question: Both carry N and F — where exactly does the difference hide?

items.answer:
The process category at each position is the same in the notation used here, but the introverted and extraverted attitudes differ.

In the writing used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se: Intuition against Intuition, Feeling against Feeling, Thinking against Thinking, Sensing against Sensing, with all four attitudes changing sides. E/I decides whether the dominant process faces out or in; J/P decides whether the outward step is perceiving or judging. The attitude of the third process is labelled differently elsewhere, so check the source when versions differ. Position describes emphasis only; it does not predict who does what first, and does not say whether the two work well together.
items.question: The function names correspond one to one — why do they come across so differently?

items.answer:
Yes. E/I describes which way attention and energy tend to turn, not how much someone talks, and not whether they can socialise.

Compare similar situations where you could choose between thinking through something privately and making sense of it in conversation. Fatigue, familiarity and assigned roles can affect either choice.
items.question: Can an INFJ be very outgoing, and an ENFP very quiet?

items.answer:
Either type can sign off on a tagline. The decision calls for judgement about the brief, audience evidence and responsibility for the final wording.

To explore the work, take three fictional taglines and write one note on options to explore and another on possible audience misunderstandings. Both are tasks anyone can try. Which one you want to practise further says more about your interest in the work than a type code does.
items.question: Which is better suited to being the final sign-off on a brand line?

items.answer:
A common sticking point is mismatched rhythm: one is still expanding while the other already wants to close, or one wants to settle while the other feels not enough has been tried.

This is not a fixed script, and either type can stand on either side. A workable agreement sets a closing point: additions allowed before it, subtractions only after, and every subtraction justified in one sentence someone else can check. In an argument, ask first who this line is for and what evidence we hold, which works better than arguing about who understands the brand. If one side discovers mid-way that the discussion must reopen, say which new piece of evidence reopens it, rather than returning to who has the final say.
items.question: Where do they most often jam on content work?

items.answer:
Not necessarily; check the item bank and the answering circumstances first.

Confirm whether both sittings used the same item set, language version and scoring definition, then review which answers were shaped by the role — being asked to give more directions, or being asked to take fewer risks. If the item bank gives dimension scores, near a boundary only means the result sits close to a threshold under this item bank; it does not show you switch naturally between two modes, and the number of candidates across a few meetings cannot replace that explanation. Leaving the result unsettled is allowed; look again in similar circumstances after a while.
